source: Hamscher, Console, de Kleer (eds.) (1992) Readings in Model-Based Diagnosis
finding: The standard reading list for model-based diagnosis (MBD). Only the Semantic Scholar record was seen, not the book text. It collects Reiter 1987 (consistency-based diagnosis from first principles) and de Kleer and Williams 1987 (GDE: conflicts, ATMS, probing).
numbers: Semantic Scholar lists 703 citations for the volume (record seen this session).
limits: Book text not opened. Content of its chapters is taken from the series' earlier subfield files, not re-read here.
agent_relevance: The reading list is the source of the ideas an agent loop could borrow: model, observations, conflicts, minimal hitting sets, and next-probe choice.

source: Sztyber-Betley, Chanthery, Trave-Massuyes, Merkelbach, Kukla, Glotin, Diedrich, Niggemann (2025) Are Diagnostic Concepts Within the Reach of LLMs? DX 2025
finding: First systematic test of LLMs on core MBD concepts: build an incidence matrix, find MSO sets, compute minimal conflicts, compute minimal diagnoses. Models: gpt-4o-mini (with code interpreter), o1, o3-mini. Tested on 23 arithmetic and logic circuits (adders, multipliers, gates), all inputs and outputs measured, component faults only.
numbers: Temp 0 for 4o-mini; reasoning effort high (Dedicated prompts) or medium (Broad prompts) for o1 and o3-mini. 10 repeats per case for 4o-mini and o3-mini; o1 run once (about $30 per iteration). o1 and o3-mini reached perfect accuracy on the incidence matrix; 4o-mini added extra variables (F1 about 0.47 for it in one metric panel). o1 best on MSO and conflicts; o3-mini best on diagnoses.
quote: at this point, LLMs do not provide an alternative to diagnosis algorithms.
limits: Each step was scored with correct inputs given, so errors do not compound. Small circuits. o1 single run. Quality varies a lot between runs. Cost and latency unbounded via API.
agent_relevance: An LLM can do single MBD steps (conflicts) well but not the full pipeline reliably. Argues for a scaffold where conflicts are checked by a deterministic tool, not trusted from the model.

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) DX 2025, prompting comparison and step difficulty
finding: Domain-rich prompts did not help. A Dedicated prompt (full MBD domain knowledge) and a Broad prompt (generic task plus definitions) gave similar MSO results. Giving the Broad prompt a correct incidence matrix as input also did not change results much. Diagnoses was the hardest step: performance fell clearly as the number of relations and diagnoses rose.
numbers: gpt-4o and gpt-4o-mini without the code interpreter gave accuracy 'close to zero on unseen examples' (footnote). Conflict F1 for circuits with zero conflicts was poor, which flattens the apparent trend. Some per-bin scores 1.00+/-0.00 for larger-conflict-count bins.
limits: Only OpenAI models. Footnote on 4o accuracy is a pilot remark, no table.
agent_relevance: More domain explanation in the prompt is not the lever. Reasoning-model effort and a code tool are. The empty-conflict case (all consistent) is a trap: models invent conflicts.

source: Plank and Wotawa (2026) Using SLMs and LLMs for Diagnosis. DX 2026
finding: 13 open or free models (3 large API models, 10 small ones from 1B to 7B) diagnose 7 systems from text descriptions: bulb circuits, heater, H-bridge powertrain, fluid heating circuit, 3-loop heater system. Scored by hand on 6 categories (0-2): correctness, completeness, reasoning, hallucination, uncertainty, clarity. Task prompt was one line: Analyze the fault scenario, what are the reasons for the fault?
numbers: Hit rate (correctness 2): Gemini 2.5 Flash 79.5%, Mistral Large 76.9%, Llama 4 Scout 17B 38.5%, Mistral 7B 25.6%, Phi-2 and TinyLlama 0.0%. Weighted score W: 1.846, 1.832, 1.526, 1.235, then down to 0.314. Hallucination rate: top three under 21% (Gemini 20.5%, Mistral Large 15.4%, Scout 7.7%); most small models over 70%; Llama 3.2 1B 94.9%. Each model ran 3 times at temp 0.2, max 800 tokens.
limits: Manual scoring, one scorer, small example systems, no commercial frontier models. Prompt did not ask for subset-minimal diagnoses.
agent_relevance: Size predicts diagnosis quality and hallucination of non-existent components. A check that every named candidate exists in the model is cheap and catches the main small-model failure.

source: Plank and Wotawa (2026) DX 2026, complexity and contamination findings
finding: Small models collapsed on the five-bulb four-switch Circuit 3 (series bulbs L3, L4 behind S3). Phi-2 scored 1.05 on the powertrain but 0.08-0.67 elsewhere; its answers ended with unrequested textbook 'Exercise' sections, so the authors read it as memory of textbook layout, not diagnosis. Large models did worse on the heating systems than on electric circuits.
numbers: Circuit 3 weighted scores: Mistral 7B 0.33, Qwen2.5 3B 0.06, Qwen2.5 1.5B 0.15, Gemini 2.5 Flash 2.00. Phi-2 powertrain 1.05. Rank-sum order equals weighted-score order for all 13 models.
limits: Authors' own explanation for Phi-2 is untested. Gemini missed some faulty components on the heater system.
agent_relevance: Familiar textbook circuits inflate scores. Test an agent on unusual component topologies, not only classic ones. Series versus parallel redundancy (needing two faults) is a good probe.

source: Plank and Wotawa (2026) DX 2026, side remark on ChatGPT
finding: In April 2026 free ChatGPT gave only correct diagnoses for the classic parallel-bulb circuit and also proposed discriminating tests (swap bulbs, voltmeter, continuity). The authors note it may rest on a built-in diagnostic procedure or on the example being widely published, and say they cannot tell which.
numbers: Single anecdote, no count.
quote: Why and how ChatGPT has these capabilities is not the focus of this paper
limits: Anecdote, not an experiment. Same circuit appears in classic MBD papers, so contamination is likely.
agent_relevance: Suggests next-probe selection (the GDE measurement step) is something chat models already imitate in prose. Whether it is correct on new systems is untested.

source: Muehlburger and Wotawa (2024) FLEX: Fault Localization and Explanation Using Open-Source LLMs in Powertrain Systems. DX 2024
finding: Open models (Mistral 7B, Llama3.1 8B, Gemma 2, Llama3) detect anomalies in battery and powertrain time series using retrieval-augmented generation. A two-step prompt (first infer operating rules from normal data, then apply the rules to find faults) fixed weak powertrain results; the original single-step prompt only worked on the battery data.
numbers: Mistral 7B F1 0.99 (precision 1.00, recall 0.98) at 1, 5 and 10 retrieved documents. Llama3 F1 0.99 with 10 documents (MMR), but F1 0.68 with 1 document (precision 0.52). Llama3.1 8B and Gemma 2 reached F1 1.0 in complex scenarios.
limits: This is anomaly detection, not component-level diagnosis. Short paper. Single dataset pair.
agent_relevance: Learning an explicit 'model' (rules) from normal behaviour before testing observations is a small scaffold-level echo of MBD (model first, then discrepancy).

source: Dave, Nguyen, Vilim (2024) Integrating LLMs for Explainable Fault Diagnosis in Complex Systems
finding: An LLM agent sits on top of PRO-AID, a consistency-based MBD tool using physics residuals and analytical redundancy relations. The LLM does not diagnose. It calls a fault_query function and explains the symbolic engine's result. Output is constrained to limit hallucination. Demonstrated on a sensor bias in a molten sodium test facility.
numbers: One demonstration: agent correctly named fault F6, a bias of a temperature sensor (TC 117), and listed the implicated sensors. No accuracy statistics.
limits: Single case. No comparison with an unaided LLM.
agent_relevance: The cleanest existing example of the 'LLM as interface, MBD engine as reasoner' split. Matches the guardrail idea of keeping the verdict in a checked tool.

source: Khan, Nahar, Chen, Constante Flores, Li (2024) FaultExplainer: LLMs for Interpretable Fault Detection and Diagnosis
finding: On the Tennessee Eastman Process, PCA flags the top contributing variables and a GPT-4o or o1-preview model names the root cause and explains it. Tested with a list of 15 known root causes, and with a general prompt (as if the fault were unseen).
numbers: With the 15-cause list, of 11 PCA-detectable faults GPT-4o classified 7 and o1-preview 9. Neither got fault 5 or fault 10. With the open general prompt both models gave a correct or related cause for 8 of 11.
limits: Aliased faults counted correct. Models can find an alternative story that fits the top six features. Occasional hallucination; relies on PCA-selected features.
agent_relevance: The stronger reasoning model gained 2 faults. Failure mode: a plausible different explanation that also fits the symptoms, so a discriminating test is needed.

source: Jha et al. (2026) Think Locally, Explain Globally: Graph-Guided LLM Investigations (EoG)
finding: IT-incident diagnosis framed as abduction over a dependency graph. An LLM only labels each visited entity as cause or symptom from a 1-hop context; a deterministic controller does traversal, state and belief propagation to return a minimal explanatory frontier. Compared to ReAct/CodeAct agents on 35 ITBench SRE scenarios, 3 runs each, high reasoning effort.
numbers: GPT-5.1 ReAct: pass@3 F1 22.9, majority@3 F1 8.6 (RC Entity). GPT-5.1 EoG: 88.9 and 86.1. GPT-OSS-120B: ReAct maj@3 F1 5.7, EoG 79.4. Kimi K2: 28.6 vs 83.0. Gemini 3 Flash: 74.3 vs 92.1. Authors state a 7x average gain in Majority@k F1.
limits: Controller code is domain-specific (about 5,000 lines of Rust). Graph is assumed available. EoG uses more input tokens (e.g. GPT-5.1 1837K vs 779K) but far fewer output tokens.
agent_relevance: The closest modern analogue of MBD conflict and fault-propagation reasoning inside an agent. Gain comes from moving state out of the model, not from a smarter prompt.

source: Jha et al. (2026) EoG ablations
finding: Asking a ReAct agent to follow the EoG algorithm in the prompt, with no external controller, collapsed consistency. Structured traversal alone gave most of the gain; belief propagation (revising earlier cause or symptom labels when new evidence arrives) added more, mostly for weaker models. Removing distributed traces made no significant change.
numbers: ReAct prompted with EoG algorithm, recall pass@3 / maj@3: GPT-5.1 40.0 / 2.9; Gemini 3 Flash 71.4 / 0.0; Kimi K2 42.9 / 0.0. Versus EoG GPT-5.1 91.4 / 88.6. Belief propagation added +6.9% (GPT-5.1) to +64.3% (GPT-OSS-120B) relative maj@3 recall over controller-only.
limits: Only 35 scenarios. 'Relative improvement' in the table mixes gains of different base sizes.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that describing a diagnostic algorithm in a prompt does not make the model run it reliably. Pass@k looks fine while majority@k is near zero. Revising earlier labels (like retracting a candidate diagnosis) has measurable value.

source: Jha, Arora, Watanabe et al. (2025) ITBench: Evaluating AI Agents across Diverse Real-World IT Automation Tasks
finding: Benchmark of 94 real IT scenarios. On Site Reliability Engineering (diagnosis plus mitigation), the best agent resolved a small share. Removing trace data cut diagnosis further. No agent solved any of the hard SRE scenarios.
numbers: gpt-4o SRE diagnosis pass@1 13.81 +/- 1.67%, mitigation 11.43 +/- 1.52%. granite-3.1-8B 3.57%, llama-3.3-70B 3.10%, llama-3.1-8B 0.99%. Without traces gpt-4o diagnosis 9.52%, mitigation 2.86%. 42 scenarios for this table (21 with traces, 21 without), 10 runs per scenario per model. Hard scenarios: 0 of 5 resolved.
limits: 2025 models; later work (c10) reports better with a different architecture. Scenario counts per table are small.
agent_relevance: Baseline showing that free-form agents do poorly at real multi-component diagnosis. Observability (how much you can measure) strongly changes outcomes, as MBD theory predicts.

source: Kim, Park, Yun, Lee (2026) Why Do AI Agents Systematically Fail at Cloud Root Cause Analysis?
finding: 1,675 OpenRCA agent runs across five models, coded into 12 failure types. Failures are shared across model tiers. Two MBD-relevant ones: Symptom-as-Cause (stopping at the first anomaly) and No Cross-Validation (single-hypothesis bias).
numbers: Overall perfect-detection accuracy 3.9% to 12.5% across five models. Hallucination in Interpretation 71.2% of runs, Incomplete Exploration 63.9%, Symptom-as-Cause 39.9% (Gemini 2.5 Pro 68.4%), No Cross-Validation 18.6%, Code generation error 27.2% (1.8% Gemini 2.5 Pro to 65.5% Claude Sonnet 4). Percentages overlap, since several can occur per run.
limits: Failure coding was done with an LLM (Opus 4.5) plus a human-defined scheme. Mitigation tests only on Claude Sonnet 4 and 70 Bank tasks.
agent_relevance: Symptom-as-Cause is the classic failure that MBD guards against by asking what else could explain the observation. Needs an explicit alternative-hypothesis step.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Cloud RCA failure analysis, mitigation experiments
finding: Prompt-level fixes failed on the main pitfalls. A hypothesis-driven template (explicit hypothesis per KPI category) broadened exploration but hallucinated interpretations stayed at similar rates. Pitfall-aware prompting did nothing useful; the agent restated the pitfalls and repeated them. An enriched Controller-Executor protocol (return code and error traces) helped.
numbers: Test on Claude Sonnet 4, 70 Bank tasks: no meaningful RCA gain from either prompt. Enriched protocol cut inter-agent pitfall rates by about 14 and 15 points (GPT-5 mini, Claude Sonnet 4); perfect detections rose GPT-5 mini 0 to 2 (0.0% to 4.9%), Gemini 2.5 Pro 1 to 3 (2.4% to 7.3%); steps -22.1% (11.9 to 9.2), tokens -1.6%, time -22.3%. A memory watcher removed all OOM crashes.
limits: Tiny absolute counts (2 to 3 successes). Bank domain only.
agent_relevance: Telling a model about hypothesis testing in the prompt does not fix interpretation errors. Structure and exposed evidence do. This matches a scaffold with external verification.

source: Wu et al. (2025) TN-AutoRCA: Benchmark and Agentic Framework for Alarm-Based Root Cause Analysis in Telecom Networks
finding: 530-scenario telecom alarm benchmark (TN-RCA530) where cause is found by reasoning over a topology and alarm graph; 94.5% of scenarios are 'Difficult'. Direct LLM prompting tops out near 59% F1. An Auto-RCA loop, where an orchestrator proposes hypothesis-driven code repairs and keeps a change only if the score does not drop, lifts F1 to 91.79%.
numbers: Best direct baseline Gemini-2.5-Pro F1 58.99%; best baseline F1@1 in Mixed scenarios 0.6254 (Qwen3-235B); final Auto-RCA F1 0.9179 (Gemini-2.5-Pro). Rounds with invalid or worse code scored 0.0000 and were rejected.
limits: Gain comes from generated search code tuned on the benchmark; generalisation to unseen networks not shown. Gemini's 1M context credited as one factor.
agent_relevance: An accept-only-if-better loop is a guard against regressions, like checking that a revised diagnosis explains more observations than before.

source: Gao, Cai, Zheng, Bai, Song (2026) One Hypothesis Is Not Enough: Abductive Reasoning with Agentic Hypothesis Refinement over Knowledge Graphs (HypoAgent)
finding: Abduction over KGs: find a first-order hypothesis whose answers explain a set of observed entities. A proposal agent calls a small trained generator, a root-cause step diagnoses why a failed hypothesis fails by running it on the graph, and the revision is then selected. Beats ReAct with KG tools and best-of-k sampling on semantic similarity across three KGs and three LLM backends.
numbers: Removing condition-update candidates lowers test Jaccard in 44.2% (BioKG), 53.0% (PharmKG8k), 33.6% (DBpedia50) of cases; removing direct rewriting, 14.0%, 15.6%, 24.0%. Ablation rows seen: w/o condition updates 0.737/0.694/0.817 vs w/o direct rewriting 0.837/0.794/0.854 (metric as in the paper's Table 7).
limits: KG hypothesis task, not device diagnosis. The ReAct KG-tool agent 'falls behind symbolic search' per authors.
agent_relevance: Same loop as MBD: propose a candidate, test it against the model, use the mismatch to revise. Gains came from diagnosis-guided repair, not more samples.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: LLM runs a hypothesis, prediction, experiment, observation, conclusion loop with a real debugger (jdb or pdb) before proposing a patch. This is the software form of discriminating tests. Repair performance matches a plain LLM, and a <DONE> signal marks when it is confident.
numbers: ARHE: plausible patches 189 (AutoSD) vs 179 (LLM-Base) vs template mean 85.77; correct 187 vs 177. Patches with <DONE> and plausible: 89% correct, versus 82% without <DONE>. If the LLM predicts the debugger output instead of running it, <DONE> predictions were 11 points less likely plausible (versus 12.4 points more likely with real execution); individual runs plausible 73% with the debugger vs 63% without.
limits: Repair gain over baseline is small and from one model class (Codex-era). Smaller models failed zero-shot (CodeGen-6B).
agent_relevance: Real execution feedback matters; a simulated experiment result hurts reliability. Supports using tools, not the model's imagination, to run each discriminating test.

source: Kang et al. (2023) AutoSD human study
finding: 20 participants (six professionals) judged patches with or without AutoSD explanations. Time was about equal; accuracy rose for five of six real bugs, but explanations can also lend credibility to wrong patches.
numbers: N=20. Accuracy higher with explanation on 5 of 6 bugs (the paper's abstract rounds this to 83% of bugs). 70% wanted explanations from repair tools; 55% were satisfied with the scientific-debugging format. Time differences not significant.
limits: Small N, mixed students and professionals. Authors flag that a coherent explanation may persuade for an incorrect patch.
agent_relevance: Explanations help human checking but can mislead. An agent's report should list rejected candidates and the test that eliminated them.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation of LLM-Based Explainable Fault Localization (AutoFL). FSE 2024
finding: LLM navigates a repository by function calls, writes a bug explanation, then names a fault location. Compared with spectrum-based fault localization (Ochiai SBFL), the classic coverage-based method also covered in this series. Repeating runs gives a confidence estimate.
numbers: 798 real bugs in Java and Python. Method-level acc@1 up 19.7% over Ochiai on Defects4J, 166.7% on BugsInPy, 233.3% on BugsInPy with GPT-4. Of 300 explanations over 60 bugs, about 20% accurately described how the bug happened; 56.7% of bugs had at least one accurate explanation.
limits: Explanations are mostly wrong or partial per sample (20% accurate). Gain is relative, not absolute. Possible training-data leak for Defects4J.
agent_relevance: LLM-based localization beats statistical ranking, but single explanations are unreliable. Repeat runs and agreement are a usable confidence signal.

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) DX 2025, positioning against earlier LLM-diagnosis work
finding: The reference list shows the small body of LLM plus MBD work as of 2025: Dave et al. 2024 (explanation over PRO-AID), Merkelbach et al. DX 2024 (multimodal LLMs to build diagnosis models), Muehlburger and Wotawa 2024 (FLEX, FaultLines), Khan et al. 2024 (FaultExplainer), Lin et al. 2025 (FD-LLM), Russell-Gilbert et al. 2024 (AAD-LLM), Kang et al. 2024 (AutoFL).
numbers: Not applicable (citation list).
limits: Only the citation entries were seen for Merkelbach, Lin, Russell-Gilbert; their results were not opened.
agent_relevance: Shows the gap: before 2025 almost all LLM work was detection or explanation. Only one paper (c02) tested conflict and diagnosis computation.

source: Plank and Wotawa (2026) DX 2026, related work statement
finding: Authors say no earlier study systematically evaluates small locally run models on text-only diagnosis with manual multi-category scoring. They contrast with Sztyber-Betley et al. (LLMs as a support tool inside a diagnosis process) and cite Qaid et al. (four open models on machine fault diagnosis said to match deep-learning methods) and Lukens et al. (LLMs with technical manuals).
numbers: Not applicable.
limits: Qaid and Lukens claims are as reported by Plank and Wotawa, not checked.
agent_relevance: Text-only diagnosis (no formal model) is the setting closest to a general agent. Results there are weaker and less stable than with formal tool support.

source: Plank and Wotawa (2026) DX 2026, consistency across runs
finding: Run-to-run noise separates model groups. The three large models have a mean standard deviation under 0.47 across the six scoring categories, most small models over 0.6.
numbers: Mean SD: Gemini 2.5 Flash 0.264, Mistral Large 0.353, Llama 4 Scout 0.467, Mistral 7B 0.653, Qwen2.5 1.5B 0.708, Gemma-2 2B 0.581. Three runs per scenario per model.
limits: Only three runs; SD of SDs not reported.
agent_relevance: Agreement across repeated runs is a cheap reliability proxy, in line with c10 (majority@k) and c19 (repeat-run confidence).

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) DX 2025, limits stated by authors
finding: Authors list costs of using LLMs in place of MBD algorithms: accuracy too low to replace the tools, API time cannot be bounded, cost, and wide run-to-run variance. They propose fine-tuning or instruction tuning and larger, hybrid or distributed benchmarks as next steps.
numbers: One o1 iteration about $30 (footnote).
limits: Opinion section.
agent_relevance: Confirms that for an agent the winning use is as a front end and checker, with exact solver steps delegated.

source: Plank and Wotawa (2026) DX 2026, which categories separate models
finding: Clarity was the strongest category for all models and hid the weakness: correctness and completeness separate good from bad models. Hallucination rate tracked the weighted score closely.
numbers: Clarity: Gemini 2.00, TinyLlama 0.64. Correctness: Gemini 1.77, Mistral Large 1.77, TinyLlama 0.28. Uncertainty (acknowledging several possible faults): Gemini 1.97, Mistral Large 1.77, Phi-2 0.28.
limits: Manual scores on a 0-2 scale; weights (30/20/20/15/10/5) set by the authors.
agent_relevance: A fluent diagnosis is not evidence of a correct one. Uncertainty over several candidates is something to score separately: MBD returns sets, not a single answer.

source: Reiter (1987) A theory of diagnosis from first principles; de Kleer and Williams (1987) Diagnosing multiple faults (as cited in c02/c20)
finding: Cited by the 2025 and 2026 LLM-diagnosis papers as the foundation: a diagnosis is a minimal hitting set of the conflict sets; Reiter's DOI appears in c02's reference list. Only the citations were seen, not the original papers.
numbers: None read.
limits: Original papers not opened this session.
agent_relevance: The formal core an agent scaffold would reproduce: conflicts from inconsistent observations, then hitting sets as candidate faults.

source: Searches run for this angle (arXiv API, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, WebSearch)
finding: Search found no arXiv paper that uses an LLM to generate conflicts for a Reiter hitting-set loop, and no paper that measures an LLM on the Readings volume's own benchmark circuits (e.g. the classic polybox or full-adder). arXiv API returned HTTP 429 and empty results; coverage is therefore incomplete.
numbers: Not applicable.
limits: Absence of evidence under rate limits. Other LLM work on spreadsheet and knowledge-base debugging belongs to the sibling subfield and was not searched here.
agent_relevance: The scaffold's MBD loop (conflicts then candidates then probe) would be untested territory in the LLM literature; claims about it need our own benchmark.
